positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds FDA's two-axis framework (device activity by consequence of an incorrect output) useful but insufficient as a complete basis for risk determination, since additional dimensions FDA itself raises — reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, traceability — plus user review capability, conversational trajectory, escalation direction, benchmark validity, subgroup behavior, third-party model change, postmarket detectability, and agentic tool use, are not represented.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework beyond two axes by incorporating the commenter's proposed 15-driver 'boundary budget' and material coupling screen, so that the additional risk-relevant dimensions are explicitly represented in risk assessment.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The commenter treats conversational trajectory and emergent behavior as risk drivers that a static activity-by-consequence grid does not capture.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment identifies user review capability and downstream safeguards as risk-relevant dimensions, framing risk as a property of the combined human-device system rather than the output alone.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: Third-party model change is listed among the drivers that must be represented in the risk framework, implying upstream model supplier behavior affects device risk.

positions.public_summary: Commenter finds FDA's two-axis activity-by-consequence risk framework useful but incomplete as a determinative test, and proposes expanding it into a 15-driver 'boundary budget' and material coupling screen covering reversibility, safeguards, time pressure, traceability, conversational trajectory, third-party model change, and agentic tool use.
positions.source_passage: The central BCR finding is that FDA's two-axis activity-by-consequence picture is useful but cannot serve as the complete closure observable. FDA itself asks whether reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, and traceability should also be represented. Other sections add user review capability, conversational trajectory, escalation direction, benchmark validity, subgroup behavior, third-party model change, postmarket detectability, and agentic tool use. BCR converts these into a 15-driver boundary budget and material coupling screen.

positions.requested_fda_action: No request is stated in the passage; it only quantifies the proportion of named risk dimensions covered by the current two-axis framework. Whether the commenter seeks expansion of the axes cannot be determined from this text.

The passage indicates additional dimensions and constraints are needed, though the terms used ("full J-vector," "couplings," "hard gates") are not explained in the passage.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter identifies four additional risk dimensions beyond the two-axis framework: time pressure/time-to-harm (a shorter response window can defeat nominal human control), reversibility (irreversible actions require hard-gate treatment), traceability/provenance (low traceability impairs auditability, attribution, and correction), and downstream safeguards (independent safeguards can suppress harmful realization).
positions.requested_fda_action: Incorporate time-to-harm, reversibility, traceability/provenance, and downstream safeguards as explicit modifiers in the risk framework, with irreversible actions subject to hard gating and traceability linked to the foundation model information (MAF) discussion.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment states that a shorter response window in time-pressured settings can defeat nominal human control, meaning human oversight cannot be assumed effective.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment ties low output traceability/provenance to impaired auditability, attribution, and correction, which concerns assigning responsibility across the chain.

positions.public_summary: Proposes expanding FDA's two-axis risk framework with four additional dimensions: time-to-harm (short response windows can defeat nominal human control), reversibility (irreversible actions warranting hard gates), traceability/provenance (affecting auditability and attribution), and independent downstream safeguards that can suppress harm.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter identifies a risk of "benchmark false-lock," in which benchmark performance is treated as automatic evidence of safety despite FDA's own acknowledgment of data contamination, saturation, and limited real-world representativeness of public benchmark assets.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat benchmark results as only one form of evidence rather than safety closure, and require a linked chain of benchmark construct validity, independent or sequestered testing, clinical confirmation, postmarket residual monitoring, and automatic re-opening of the assessment after any safety-relevant change.
positions.public_summary: Accepts benchmarking as part of evaluation but warns against treating benchmark performance as automatic safety closure given contamination and saturation. Asks FDA to require construct validity, independent or sequestered testing, clinical confirmation, postmarket monitoring, and automatic reassessment after safety-relevant changes.
positions.source_passage:
The second central finding is benchmark false-lock. FDA explicitly recognizes contamination, saturation, and limited real-world
representativeness of public benchmark assets. BCR therefore treats benchmark performance as one witness, never as
automatic safety closure. The repair chain is benchmark construct validity -> independent/sequestered testing -> clinical
confirmation -> postmarket residual monitoring -> automatic re-open after safety-relevant change.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter appears concerned that the level of clinical confirmation should be driven by whichever risk pathway remains unresolved after earlier evidence, rather than by a generic risk tier, and that testing must be clinically representative to close remaining intended-use uncertainties.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt the tiered clinical confirmation ladder (retrospective, shadow, standardized, adjudicated, prospective) but scale the required rung to the highest-risk unresolved evidentiary branch, and require clinically representative testing conditions to resolve residual intended-use uncertainty.
positions.public_summary: Brief, outline-form comment endorsing FDA's graduated clinical confirmation approach while proposing that the required evidence tier be set by the highest-risk unresolved question, with clinically representative testing used to resolve remaining intended-use uncertainties. Terse phrasing limits interpretation.
positions.source_passage:
S7 Clinical confirmation ladder Escalate evidence from retrospective/shadow/standardized/adjudicated/prospective methods based on the highest-risk unresolved branch.
Clinically representative witness closes intended-use residuals.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter considers FDA's activity and consequence dimensions useful but insufficient on their own, warning that a two-dimensional visualization could substitute for the fuller set of factors and couplings that actually determine regulatory outcomes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the activity and consequence dimensions but situate them within a broader multi-dimensional set of boundary factors (described as a 15-element boundary vector plus material couplings) rather than treating the two-axis chart as the complete risk framework.
positions.public_summary: Commenter finds FDA's activity and consequence axes useful but incomplete, urging that they be embedded in a broader multi-dimensional set of boundary factors and their interactions, so the two-axis visualization does not substitute for fuller risk characterization.
positions.source_passage: 15.1 Boundary vector. FDA's activity and consequence dimensions remain useful, but the closure object is the broader boundary vector J={J1...J15} plus material couplings. This prevents the two-dimensional visualization from replacing the actual regulatory realization problem.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Certain safety failures are not commensurable with aggregate performance metrics, so favorable average results could mask categorically unacceptable events such as irreversible or unauthorized actions, catastrophic missed escalations, dependency identity mismatches, or failure of required human intervention.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add a prespecified 'hard-gate' overlay to the risk/evidence framework under which any occurrence of a defined non-averagable safety event prevents the affected release or use slice from closing, regardless of favorable aggregate metrics.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The proposal treats unauthorized or irreversible high-consequence actions and catastrophic missed escalations as categorical failures rather than events absorbed into averaged performance.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It designates failure of required human intervention or confirmation as a gating event, framing safety as a property of the combined human-AI workflow rather than model output alone.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: 'Dependency identity mismatch' is listed as a hard-gate trigger, treating unverified underlying model or component identity as a disqualifying safety condition.

positions.public_summary: Proposes supplementing FDA's risk and evidence framework with a prespecified 'hard-gate' overlay: defined non-averagable events—unauthorized or unconfirmed irreversible actions, catastrophic missed escalations, dependency identity mismatches, or failed required human intervention—would block release of the affected slice despite favorable aggregate performance metrics.
positions.source_passage: 15.3 Hard-gate overlay. Define a prespecified hard-gate event H=1 for any non-averagable safety branch such as an unauthorized high-consequence action, an irreversible action without required confirmation, a catastrophic missed escalation above its allowable limit, a dependency identity mismatch, or failure of required human intervention. When H=1, the affected release/use slice cannot close regardless of favorable aggregate metrics.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Under-escalation and over-escalation errors are not commensurable; combining them into a single aggregate risk metric could mask severe under-escalation harms even when overall error rates appear acceptable.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that residual risk for under-escalation and over-escalation be reported separately, characterized by severity and timing, and permit collapsing them into a single scalar only when clinical weighting is prospectively justified; allow severe under-escalation to function as a hard acceptance gate.
positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's attention to both escalation error directions but asks that under- and over-escalation residual risks be tracked separately with severity and timing, not combined into one scalar absent prospective clinical justification, with severe under-escalation usable as a hard acceptance gate.
positions.source_passage: 15.4 Two-direction escalation residuals. Keep R_under and R_over separate with severity and timing. Do not collapse them into one scalar unless the clinical weighting is prospectively justified. Severe under-escalation can remain a hard gate even if over-escalation is low.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket modifications and third-party dependency updates shift the device's defined boundaries, and that requalification should be scoped to what actually changed rather than applied uniformly, while safety-critical ('hard-gate') pathways should never be exempt from direct re-evidence.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a change-control approach in which any modification or third-party dependency update is treated as a defined boundary delta, with requalification scope scaled to the changed interfaces and their material couplings, and with hard-gate branches always requiring direct re-evidence; PCCP would then function as a controlled envelope of permitted boundary movement.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposal reframes PCCP as a bounded envelope of allowable movement in the device's declared boundaries, addressing behavioral drift beyond a static prespecified change list.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: It treats third-party dependency updates as change events that trigger scoped requalification, addressing supplier-initiated changes outside the manufacturer's control.

positions.public_summary: Accepts PCCP-based change control but proposes a specific structure: treat each modification or third-party dependency update as a defined boundary delta, scale requalification to the changed interfaces and their material couplings, and always require direct re-evidence for safety-critical branches.
positions.source_passage: 15.6 Change delta. A postmarket modification or third-party dependency update creates a boundary delta, Delta J. Requalification scope follows the changed J_i and material J_iJ_j couplings, while hard-gate branches always receive direct re-evidence. This turns PCCP into a controlled envelope of allowable boundary movement.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Combining benchmark, clinical, synthetic, and postmarket evidence into a single performance estimate risks obscuring differences in the underlying data sources; the commenter treats these as distinct evidence streams whose pooling must be justified rather than assumed.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require sponsors to demonstrate independence and transportability across evidence sources before any pooling, and should not permit synthetic and real-world data to be merged into one performance estimate merely because both exist.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses combining evidence types, stating benchmark, clinical, synthetic, and postmarket data should be treated as separate evidence streams unless independence and transportability are demonstrated, and opposing merging synthetic and real-world data into a single performance estimate simply because both are available.
positions.source_passage: 15.7 Evidence fusion. Benchmark, clinical, synthetic, and postmarket evidence remain distinct witnesses until independence and transportability are demonstrated. Synthetic and real-world data should not be merged into one performance estimate solely because both are available.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the two-axis activity-by-consequence matrix as insufficient on its own to close out risk, treating it as a communication device rather than a complete risk determination model, and identifies additional risk-relevant dimensions it does not capture (including reversibility, downstream safeguards, time-to-harm, traceability, user review capability, conversational trajectory, model/dependency change, subgroup performance, tool permissions, and postmarket detectability).
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the two-axis matrix as a communication layer while requiring a mandatory 'boundary ledger' documenting the additional listed dimensions, and overlay hard gates for irreversible or catastrophic risk branches.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposed ledger includes conversational trajectory as a risk dimension, implying risk depends on emergent behavior across an exchange rather than a static intended use statement.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The commenter lists model/dependency change as a risk dimension requiring documentation, extending risk assessment to upstream model and dependency shifts.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: Tool permissions and irreversible-branch hard gates are proposed as explicit risk dimensions, addressing how much action authority is delegated to the system.

positions.public_summary: Accepts the two-axis activity-by-consequence matrix only as a communication layer, not a complete risk model.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 1 - Risk framework dimensions
...
BCR response. Use the activity x consequence matrix as a communication layer, not the full closure model. Add a mandatory boundary ledger for reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure/time-to-harm, traceability/provenance, user review capability, conversational trajectory, model/dependency change, subgroup performance, tool permissions, and postmarket detectability. Overlay hard gates for irreversible or catastrophic branches.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that assessing directiveness through fixed wording or keyword-based tests would miss how much pressure to act an output actually exerts, since directiveness accumulates across an interaction rather than residing in a single phrase.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should define directiveness as realized action pressure across the whole interaction and evaluate it using multiple modifiers—specificity, personalization, imperative force, immediacy, repetition, preservation of alternatives, and consequence—assessed over realistic conversational trajectories.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment frames directiveness as something that emerges cumulatively across an interaction trajectory rather than as a fixed property of a single output, implying risk must be assessed over a behavioral envelope.

positions.public_summary: Responding to Q2, the commenter accepts a continuum view of directiveness but urges FDA to define it as realized action pressure across an entire interaction rather than a keyword test, assessed via specificity, personalization, imperative force, immediacy, repetition, preserved alternatives, and consequence over realistic trajectories.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 2 - Spectrum of informational directiveness
...
BCR response. Treat directiveness as realized action pressure across the interaction, not a keyword test. Evaluate specificity, personalization, imperative force, immediacy, repetition, preservation of alternatives, and consequence across realistic trajectories.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that classifying risk by whether a user is a patient or an HCP does not establish that use is safe, since actual user comprehension and response to outputs vary, including across health-literacy levels.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require empirical measurement of whether intended users understand device limitations, detect plausible errors, respond appropriately to uncertainty, and follow escalation instructions across health-literacy levels, rather than inferring safety from patient vs. HCP labels.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment shifts evaluation from the device's user category to measured user behavior—comprehension, error detection, and escalation response—making the human-device combination the unit of assessment.

positions.public_summary: Addressing patient- versus HCP-facing risk, the commenter argues user-category labels alone should not be treated as evidence of safe use. It asks FDA to require measurement of whether intended users grasp limitations, spot plausible errors, handle uncertainty, and follow escalation instructions across health-literacy levels.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 3 - Patient-facing vs HCP-facing risk
...
BCR response. Do not infer safe use solely from patient/HCP labels. Measure whether intended users understand limitations, detect plausible errors, respond to uncertainty, and act on escalation instructions across health-literacy levels.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Framing risk around the generalist/specialist professional distinction is too coarse; what matters is whether the specific task exceeds the user's competency for the output at hand.
positions.requested_fda_action: Assess risk based on task-to-competency mismatch rather than professional title alone, and where safety depends on specialty knowledge, require validation of the generalist user's independent review of outputs and of the device's specialist-escalation behavior.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment asks that validation cover the generalist user's ability to independently review device output, i.e., the clinician-device combination rather than the device alone.

positions.public_summary: Supports considering generalist versus specialist use but argues risk should turn on task-to-competency mismatch rather than professional title. Where safety depends on specialty knowledge, urges FDA to require validation of the generalist's independent review of outputs and of the device's specialist-escalation behavior.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 4 - Generalist vs specialist HCP use
...
BCR response. Base risk on task-to-competency mismatch, not professional title alone. If safety depends on specialty knowledge, validate the generalist's independent review and the device's specialist-escalation behavior.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Assessing single outputs in isolation would miss how a conversational device's behavior shifts over the course of an exchange, including migration from non-directive to action-directing or action-taking states, order effects, long-context degradation, and cumulative drift beyond intended boundaries.
positions.requested_fda_action: Evaluate the entire multi-turn conversation as a state trajectory rather than as discrete outputs, tracking transitions toward action-directing/action-taking behavior, order effects, long-context performance degradation, and cumulative boundary drift.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment frames the device's behavior as drifting across a conversation beyond its stated boundaries, implying intended use must be defined as a behavioral envelope tracked over trajectories rather than a fixed output-level claim.

positions.public_summary: Responding on multi-turn conversational devices, the commenter urges FDA to assess the full conversation as a state trajectory rather than isolated outputs, tracking migration from non-directive to action-directing or action-taking states, order effects, long-context degradation, and cumulative boundary drift.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 5 - Multi-turn conversational trajectories
...
BCR response. Evaluate the entire conversation as a state trajectory. Track migration from non-directive to action-directing/action-taking states, order effects, long-context degradation, and cumulative boundary drift.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Combining under-escalation and over-escalation errors into a single composite metric could obscure clinically distinct failure modes that differ in severity and timing.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to report under- and over-escalation residuals separately, characterized by severity and timing, and permit aggregation into one score only where a clinical weighting rule is justified in advance; treat severe missed escalation as a potential hard acceptance gate.
positions.public_summary: Accepts evaluating both error directions but asks FDA to keep under- and over-escalation metrics separate, reported with severity and timing, allowing a combined score only with a pre-justified clinical weighting rule, and treating severe missed escalation as a possible hard gate.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 6 - Under- vs over-escalation
...
BCR response. Maintain separate under- and over-escalation residuals with severity and timing. Do not force them into one score unless a clinical weighting rule is justified in advance; severe missed escalation can be a hard gate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts the competency-based approach only if benchmarking, clinical confirmation, and postmarket monitoring are linked as a single continuous chain of evidence, and only if that evidence corresponds to the exact configuration actually deployed rather than a test-stage version.
positions.requested_fda_action: Structure the competency-based framework so that benchmarking, clinical confirmation, and postmarket monitoring form one continuous closure chain, with evidence explicitly tied to the final deployed device configuration.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment conditions support on evidence being tied to the exact final deployed configuration, raising the question of how premarket assurance carries over to what is actually fielded.

positions.public_summary: Finds the competency-based approach useful, but conditions support on benchmarking, clinical confirmation, and postmarket monitoring forming a single continuous closure chain, with evidence tied to the exact final deployed device configuration rather than a tested variant.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 7 - Competency-based premarket approach
...
BCR response. The competency-based model is useful if benchmark -> clinical confirmation -> postmarket monitoring forms one continuous closure chain tied to the exact final deployed configuration.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that averaging or aggregating risk across the two axes could understate evidence needs when specific hazardous conditions are present, such as irreversibility of resulting actions, tool actions hidden from the user, poor observability, or severe subgroup performance failures.
positions.requested_fda_action: Use device activity and consequence only for initial risk tiering, then scale evidence using a fuller set of boundary factors plus 'hard gates' that prevent a low average risk position from reducing evidence requirements when irreversibility, hidden tool action, poor observability, or severe subgroup failure is present.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The comment treats irreversibility of actions and poor observability as risk factors that must independently drive evidence requirements, beyond the consequence-of-incorrect-output axis.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It singles out 'hidden tool action'—the device acting through tools without user visibility—as a condition that should trigger a non-waivable evidence gate.

positions.public_summary: Accepts activity and consequence as an initial tiering basis, but asks FDA to scale evidence using a broader set of risk factors and to apply hard gates so that irreversibility, hidden tool action, poor observability, or severe subgroup failure cannot be averaged away.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 8 - Risk framework used to scale evidence
...
BCR response. Use activity and consequence for initial tiering, then scale evidence using the full boundary vector and hard gates. A low average position cannot reduce evidence when irreversibility, hidden tool action, poor observability, or severe subgroup failure exists.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views FDA's ten proposed benchmark elements as a sound core but incomplete, omitting checks on model provenance and dependency identity, sensitivity to underlying model changes, human override, reversibility, tool permissions, extended interaction trajectories, and whether benchmarks are valid and uncontaminated.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the ten benchmark elements but add explicit benchmarking gates for provenance/dependency identity, model-change sensitivity, meaningful human override, reversibility/rollback, tool permissions, long trajectories, and benchmark construct validity/contamination.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment asks for benchmark gates on provenance/dependency identity and sensitivity to changes in the underlying model, which concerns assurance over upstream model suppliers rather than benchmark content alone.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It calls for a gate on meaningful human override, testing the clinician-device system rather than the model in isolation.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It seeks gates on tool permissions, long trajectories, and reversibility/rollback, addressing how much action authority the system is granted.

positions.public_summary: Comment finds FDA's ten benchmarking elements a strong core but incomplete, requesting added explicit gates covering model provenance and dependency identity, sensitivity to model changes, meaningful human override, reversibility and rollback, tool permissions, long interaction trajectories, and benchmark construct validity and contamination.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 9 - Adequacy of benchmarking elements
...
BCR response. FDA's ten benchmark elements are a strong core. Add explicit gates for provenance/dependency identity, model-change sensitivity, meaningful human override, reversibility/rollback, tool permissions, long trajectories, and benchmark construct validity/contamination.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Benchmark results may not predict real-world, intended-use behavior unless construct validity is demonstrated and contamination, representativeness, and stability concerns are addressed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to provide evidence linking benchmark performance to intended-use behavior, including independent or sequestered benchmark assets, contamination controls, representative case morphology, subgroup and trajectory coverage, perturbation stability testing, and correlation with clinical and postmarket observations.
positions.public_summary: Supports benchmarking with added conditions: FDA should require demonstrated construct validity, using independent or sequestered assets, contamination controls, representative and subgroup/trajectory coverage, perturbation stability testing, and correlation with clinical and postmarket evidence before benchmarks are relied upon.
positions.source_passage:

...
BCR response. Require evidence that benchmark performance predicts intended-use behavior: independent/sequestered assets, contamination controls, representative morphology, subgroup/trajectory coverage, perturbation stability, and correlation with clinical/postmarket witnesses.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Confirmation rigor should be calibrated to the most consequential behavior a device can actually realize, not to an average or nominal use, so that high-consequence or autonomous functions are not cleared on weaker evidence.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a sequential clinical-confirmation ladder keyed to the highest-risk realized branch of device behavior: allow retrospective or shadow evidence to close lower-risk informational uses, while requiring clinically representative confirmation, potentially including prospective study, for high-consequence or autonomous uses.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: Anchoring evidence rigor to the "highest-risk realized branch" treats the device's achievable behavioral envelope, rather than a fixed nominal intended use, as the basis for validation.

positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's tiered approach to clinical confirmation but asks that rigor be set by the highest-risk behavior a device can actually realize: retrospective or shadow evidence for lower-risk informational uses, clinically representative or prospective study for high-consequence or autonomous uses.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 11 - Selecting clinical-confirmation rigor
...
BCR response. Use a sequential clinical-confirmation ladder based on the highest-risk realized branch. Lower-risk informational uses may close with retrospective/shadow evidence; high-consequence or autonomous uses need stronger clinically representative confirmation and may require prospective study.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Performance estimates for GenAI devices may be statistically ill-defined or misleading if analytic choices are not fixed in advance, and pooling synthetic with real-world data could obscure true performance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to prespecify estimands, denominators, subgroup and conversational-trajectory strata, uncertainty intervals, and missing-data rules, and to report synthetic and real-world estimates separately unless distributional transportability and lineage independence are demonstrated to justify combining them.
positions.public_summary: Responding to Q12, the commenter urges prespecification of estimands, denominators, subgroup and trajectory strata, uncertainty intervals, and missing-data rules, and would keep synthetic and real-world performance estimates separate unless distributional transportability and lineage independence justify combining them.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 12 - Statistically meaningful performance; synthetic/real evidence
...
BCR response. Prespecify estimands, denominators, subgroup/trajectory strata, uncertainty intervals, and missing-data rules. Keep synthetic and real estimates separate unless distributional transportability and lineage independence justify combination.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Synthetic data is useful for combinatorial stress testing, rare known scenarios, perturbations, and privacy-constrained coverage, but cannot detect unknown blind spots and may reproduce correlated performance gaps when the generator and the device under evaluation share the same weaknesses.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit synthetic data only as a bounded supplement — not as sole support for safety-critical claims or unknown blind spots — and require independent real-world sentinel data plus disclosure of synthetic data lineage.
positions.public_summary: Supports synthetic data for combinatorial stress testing, rare known scenarios, perturbations, and privacy-limited coverage, but not as sole evidence for safety-critical claims or unknown blind spots given correlated generator-device gaps. Asks FDA to require independent real-world sentinel data and synthetic data lineage disclosure.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 13 - Where synthetic data helps or fails
...
BCR response. Use synthetic data for combinatorial stress, rare known scenarios, perturbations, and privacy-constrained coverage; do not rely on it alone for unknown blind spots or safety-critical claims where generator and device may share correlated gaps. Add independent real sentinels and lineage disclosure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The comparator and acceptance criteria should be derived from the device's intended use and the counterfactual workflow it would replace or alter, rather than a default comparator. The commenter also implies that device-alone and human-AI team performance are distinct questions that should not be collapsed into one.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should have sponsors select comparators based on intended use and the counterfactual workflow, apply an appropriate clinical standard where substitution is claimed, and evaluate human-AI team performance and device-alone performance as separate assessments when both are relevant.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The commenter treats human-AI team performance and device-alone performance as separate measurements that may both be required, rather than an either/or choice as FDA's question frames it.

positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's comparator framing but recommends selecting comparators from the device's intended use and the counterfactual workflow, applying an appropriate clinical standard for substitution claims, and testing human-AI team and device-alone performance separately when both are relevant.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 14 - Comparator and acceptance criteria
...
BCR response. Choose the comparator from intended use and counterfactual workflow. Use an appropriate clinical standard for substitution claims; test human-AI team and device-alone performance separately when both matter.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that performance comparisons should reflect the care patients would actually receive if the device were not used, rather than an idealized benchmark.
positions.requested_fda_action: Allow and include the actual counterfactual as a comparator, specifying options such as unaided clinician judgment, delayed specialist review, alternative technology, or no intervention where clinically appropriate.
positions.public_summary: The commenter agrees with FDA that performance may be assessed against the care likely to occur without the device, and would include counterfactual comparators such as unaided clinicians, delayed specialist review, alternative technology, or no intervention when clinically appropriate.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 15 - Compare to care absent the device
...
BCR response. Yes - include the actual counterfactual care likely without the device: unaided clinician, delayed specialist review, alternative technology, or no intervention when clinically appropriate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Third-party involvement is seen as valuable for functions requiring independence—sequestered test data, red-teaming, adjudication, and benchmark upkeep—but only if qualification and conflict-of-interest rules are transparent and the market for such services is not concentrated in a single provider.
positions.requested_fda_action: Involve qualified independent third parties in sequestered dataset custody, red-team testing, adjudication, and benchmark maintenance, and pair this with transparent qualification and conflict rules, multiple eligible providers, rotation among them, and retest/appeal mechanisms.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment would place evaluation-critical functions such as sequestered testing, adjudication, and benchmark maintenance in the hands of external parties, raising the need for qualification, conflict, rotation, and appeal controls over that delegated role.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: Calling for multiple eligible providers, rotation, and benchmark maintenance implies an ongoing assessment infrastructure that must scale beyond a single one-time review.

positions.public_summary: Supports using qualified independent third parties for sequestered datasets, red-team testing, adjudication, and benchmark maintenance. Conditions this on transparent qualification and conflict-of-interest rules, multiple eligible providers, rotation among them, and retest and appeal mechanisms.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 16 - Independent third parties
...
BCR response. Use qualified independent third parties for sequestered datasets, red-team testing, adjudication, and benchmark maintenance, with transparent qualification/conflict rules, multiple eligible providers, rotation, and retest/appeal mechanisms.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that a single technology-neutral evaluation/closure architecture is workable but does not by itself address failure modes specific to particular model architectures, such as multimodal inconsistency, long-horizon state error in world models, loss of clinically relevant morphology, and unverified actions by autonomous controllers.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain a technology-neutral closure architecture while adding architecture-specific failure branches covering multimodal consistency, world-model state/long-horizon error, clinically relevant morphology preservation, and action-state verification for autonomous controllers.
positions.public_summary: Supports keeping the evaluation architecture technology-neutral, but asks FDA to add architecture-specific failure branches: multimodal consistency, world-model state and long-horizon error, preservation of clinically relevant morphology, and action-state verification for autonomous controllers.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 17 - Other model architectures
...
BCR response. Keep the closure architecture technology-neutral but add architecture-specific failure branches: multimodal consistency, world-model state/long-horizon error, clinically relevant morphology preservation, and action-state verification for autonomous controllers.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that shifting evidence generation to the postmarket phase is only defensible when residual risk is bounded and failures can actually be detected and corrected before patients are harmed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit greater premarket uncertainty only where residual risk is bounded, detectability is demonstrated, monitoring is sensitive, intervention occurs before unacceptable harm, and resulting actions are reversible or otherwise controlled; exclude catastrophic, irreversible, or poorly observable risks from postmarket deferral.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment conditions postmarket reliance on proven detectability and monitoring sensitivity in deployment, raising whether such assurance capability can actually be demonstrated and sustained in the field.

positions.public_summary: Accepts greater reliance on postmarket monitoring only under conditions: bounded residual risk, demonstrated detectability, sensitive monitoring, intervention before unacceptable harm, and reversible or controlled actions. Argues catastrophic, irreversible, or poorly observable risks should not be deferred to the postmarket phase.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 18 - Greater postmarket reliance / premarket uncertainty
...
BCR response. Allow greater postmarket reliance only when residuals are bounded, detectability is proven, monitoring is sensitive, intervention precedes unacceptable harm, and actions are reversible or otherwise controlled. Do not defer catastrophic, irreversible, or poorly observable risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Postmarket reassessment based on a fixed schedule alone would not capture changes that arise between review intervals, such as upstream model or dependency updates, distribution shifts, subgroup degradation, or near-miss events.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a postmarket framework that uses both calendar-based cadence and defined event triggers (model/dependency update, distribution shift, complaint or adverse-event signal, subgroup degradation, tool change, safety-metric drift, near-miss), and combine re-benchmarking, clinician review, telemetry, outcomes data, and sentinel cases.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The commenter identifies updates to underlying models, dependencies, and tools as events that should trigger postmarket reassessment, pointing to reliance on upstream suppliers not fully addressed by the cadence question as framed.

positions.public_summary: Endorses FDA's postmarket approaches but asks that reassessment be driven by both calendar cadence and specific event triggers—model or dependency updates, distribution shift, adverse-event signals, subgroup degradation, tool changes, metric drift, near-misses—combining re-benchmarking, clinician review, telemetry, outcomes, and sentinel cases.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 19 - Postmarket approaches and cadence
...
BCR response. Use both calendar cadence and event triggers: model/dependency update, distribution shift, complaint/adverse-event signal, subgroup degradation, tool change, safety-metric drift, or near-miss. Combine rebenchmarking, clinician review, telemetry, outcomes, and sentinel cases.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Machine-based supervisory agents could be relied upon to validate the device they oversee, and their own detection performance and shared blind spots may go unexamined.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit supervisory agents only in an assisting role, not as self-certification: require independent validation of the supervisor, version/lineage control, measured detection performance, testing for common-mode blind spots, audit logs, and fail-safe human escalation.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses limits on delegating oversight functions to an automated supervisor, insisting it cannot self-certify the device and must escalate to humans.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It raises assurance requirements for the monitoring layer itself, including version/lineage control, detection performance measurement, and common-mode blind-spot testing.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents as an aid to postmarket monitoring but not as self-certification of the device. Asks FDA to require independent validation of the supervisor, version and lineage control, measured detection performance, common-mode blind-spot testing, audit logs, and fail-safe human escalation.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 20 - Machine-based supervisory agents
...
BCR response. Machine supervisors may assist but should not self-certify the device. Validate them independently, control their version/lineage, measure detection performance, test common-mode blind spots, maintain audit logs, and provide fail-safe human escalation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that involving clinicians, institutions, professional societies, and standards bodies in postmarket monitoring could dilute manufacturer responsibility unless evidence-generation roles are separated from accountability.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should structure ecosystem roles so that evidence generation is distributed while accountability remains with the manufacturer, which retains a master residual/closure ledger, with clinicians and institutions supplying witness evidence, societies supplying clinical standards, and standards bodies supporting interoperable evidence structures.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment directly addresses how responsibility should be allocated across manufacturers, clinicians, institutions, and standards bodies, proposing a manufacturer-held ledger as the mechanism to keep accountability undiffused.

positions.public_summary: Supports shared ecosystem participation in postmarket monitoring but proposes that only evidence generation be distributed: manufacturers would retain a master residual/closure ledger and accountability, while clinicians and institutions supply witness evidence, societies supply clinical standards, and standards bodies support interoperable evidence structures.
positions.source_passage:
FDA Question 21 - Shared ecosystem roles without diffusing accountability
...
BCR response. Distribute evidence generation, not accountability. The manufacturer should retain the master residual/closure ledger; clinicians/institutions supply witnesses, societies supply clinical standards, and standards bodies support interoperable evidence structures.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Machine-based supervisory agents could be relied upon to attest to a device's own performance without independent evidence, and a supervisor may share blind spots with the device it monitors.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit supervisory agents only in an assistive role, not as self-certification, and require independent validation of the supervisor, version/lineage control, measured detection performance, common-mode blind-spot testing, audit logs, and fail-safe human escalation, with re-evaluation triggered by supervisor/device updates or detection degradation.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses limits on delegating oversight to an automated supervisor, stating it may assist but must not self-certify the device and must itself be independently evidenced.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It conditions automated supervision on a fail-safe human escalation path, treating the supervisor-plus-human arrangement rather than the agent alone as the unit of assurance.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents in an assisting role for postmarket monitoring but not as self-certification. Asks FDA to require independent validation of the supervisor, version control, measured detection performance, testing for shared blind spots, audit logs, human fail-safe escalation, and re-evaluation after updates or degradation.
positions.source_passage:
Machine supervisors may assist but should not self-certify the device. Validate them independently, control their version/lineage, measure detection performance, test common-mode blind spots, maintain audit logs, and provide fail-safe human escalation.
BCR rule basis. BCR-R06,R08,R11,R13,R15
...
Closure evidence. Independent supervisor validation, version control, detection performance, common-mode testing, human fail-safe
Pass / re-open. Supervisor is independently evidenced and shared-blind-spot risk is tested Re-open when: Supervisor/device update or detection degradation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: That involving clinicians, institutions, professional societies, and standards bodies in postmarket evidence generation could diffuse responsibility if roles are not formally separated from ownership of residual risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Structure postmarket monitoring so evidence generation is distributed while accountability is not: require the manufacturer to maintain a master residual/closure ledger with a single named accountable owner for each residual, with external contributors supplying traceable witnesses, societies supplying clinical standards, and standards bodies supporting interoperable evidence structures.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment directly addresses how responsibility can be kept singular and traceable when multiple external parties contribute postmarket evidence, proposing a named accountable owner per residual risk.

positions.public_summary: Supports multi-stakeholder postmarket roles but asks FDA to separate distributed evidence generation from accountability: manufacturers would hold a master residual/closure ledger with one named accountable owner per residual, while clinicians, institutions, societies, and standards bodies supply traceable witnesses, clinical standards, and interoperable evidence structures.
positions.source_passage:
BCR response. Distribute evidence generation, not accountability. The manufacturer should retain the master residual/closure ledger; clinicians/institutions supply witnesses, societies supply clinical standards, and standards bodies support interoperable evidence structures.
...
Closure evidence. Master residual ledger with named accountable owner; external contributors provide traceable witnesses
Pass / re-open. Every residual has one accountable owner despite distributed evidence generation

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's concern is that re-evaluation scope for post-deployment modifications should be tied systematically to which behavioral boundaries a change affects, rather than treated uniformly, so that low-impact changes are not over-tested while changes to models, tools, intended use, permissions, or safety behaviors receive broad revalidation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a tiered classification of modifications by 'boundary delta': cosmetic/non-safety UI changes managed within the quality management system, prompt/retrieval changes requiring targeted requalification, and model/tool/intended-use/permission/safety-behavior changes requiring broad revalidation, with direct regression evidence always required for hard-gate branches and closure documented via change-delta records, affected-branch regression, hold/release decisions, and hard-gate retests.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposal defines modification significance in terms of changes to a device's behavioral boundaries—including permissions, safety behaviors, and intended use—implying the regulated envelope is a set of behavioral limits that must be re-verified when shifted.

positions.public_summary: Accepts using the premarket baseline for re-evaluating changes, but proposes scaling requalification by "boundary delta": cosmetic UI changes within the quality system, prompt/retrieval changes needing targeted retesting, and model, tool, intended-use, permission, or safety-behavior changes needing broad revalidation, with regression evidence for hard-gate branches.
positions.source_passage:
BCR response. Classify modification by boundary delta. Cosmetic/non-safety UI changes may stay within QMS; prompt/retrieval changes require targeted requalification; model/tool/intended-use/permission/safety-behavior changes can require broad revalidation. Hard-gate branches always receive direct regression evidence.
...
Closure evidence. Change delta record, affected-branch regression, hold/release decision, hard-gate retest
Pass / re-open. Requalification scope is traceable to changed boundaries and passes affected gates

positions.stakeholder_concern: Because the exact scope of future GenAI modifications cannot be enumerated in advance, change-control approaches that require prespecifying each individual edit would not work; the commenter is concerned with keeping changes inside a validated, testable boundary.
positions.requested_fda_action: Allow PCCPs to prespecify an allowable change envelope—which boundaries may move, maximum deltas, required tests, hold points, rollback conditions, and new-submission triggers—so changes inside the envelope that pass required tests may be released, while changes outside the envelope or failed tests require re-review.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment reframes change control around a validated behavioral/change envelope with movable boundaries and maximum deltas rather than enumerated modifications, addressing device behavior that shifts within limits over time.

positions.public_summary: Accepts adapting PCCP concepts to GenAI but urges FDA to permit prespecification of an allowable change envelope—movable boundaries, maximum deltas, required tests, hold points, rollback conditions, and new-submission triggers—rather than each exact future modification, with re-review when changes fall outside the envelope or tests fail.
positions.source_passage:
BCR response. Prespecify an allowable change envelope rather than every exact future edit: which boundaries may move, maximum deltas, required tests, hold points, rollback conditions, and new-submission triggers.
...
Pass / re-open. Change remains inside validated envelope and required tests pass before release Re-open when: Change outside envelope or failed control/test.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Third-party model changes initiated by the foundation model developer may go undetected by the device sponsor, leaving safety-relevant dependency changes unmanaged.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect sponsors to combine contractual change-notification with technical detection (version identifiers/fingerprints, canary probes, shadow/delta testing, API behavior checks) plus change quarantine, rollback, and requalification, and treat the assurance argument as unresolved if a sponsor cannot detect a safety-relevant dependency change.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment centers on assuring quality and change transparency from an upstream foundation model supplier through contractual and technical controls rather than trusting developer disclosure alone.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It proposes ongoing operational mechanisms—canary probes, shadow/delta tests, quarantine, rollback, and requalification—needed to maintain assurance of a deployed device as its dependencies change.

positions.public_summary: Endorses combining contractual change notification with technical detection of third-party model changes—version fingerprints, canary probes, shadow/delta tests, API behavior checks—plus change quarantine, rollback, and requalification, and argues the assurance case remains open if a sponsor cannot detect safety-relevant dependency changes.
positions.source_passage: BCR response. Use contractual notification plus technical detection: version identifiers/fingerprints, canary probes, shadow/delta tests, API behavior checks, change quarantine, rollback, and requalification. If the sponsor cannot detect a safety-relevant dependency change, the branch is not closed.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Voluntary Foundation Model MAFs are only useful if they are kept current, versioned, and genuinely safety-relevant; because participation is voluntary, information gaps will persist and cannot substitute for a sponsor's own assurance over its model dependency.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt the MAF concept but specify required content—architecture and interface boundaries, training-data provenance, supported uses, known limitations and failure modes, subgroup evaluations, guardrails, version history, update commitments, and audit-log availability—while acknowledging voluntary coverage gaps and continuing to require sponsors to independently assure their foundation model dependencies.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment frames the foundation model as a supplied component requiring documented provenance, versioning, limitations, and update commitments, plus independent sponsor verification of that supplier input.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: It stresses that voluntary disclosure by model developers leaves explicit gaps, so responsibility for dependency assurance still rests with the device sponsor.

positions.public_summary: Supports voluntary Foundation Model Master Files if kept current and versioned, and specifies content such as interface boundaries, training-data provenance, limitations, subgroup evaluations, guardrails, version history, and audit logs. Notes voluntary participation leaves gaps; sponsors still need independent dependency assurance.
positions.source_passage: BCR response. Foundation Model MAFs can help if current, versioned, and safety-relevant. Include architecture/interface boundaries, appropriate training-data provenance, supported uses, known limitations/failure modes, subgroup evaluations, guardrails, version history, update commitments, and audit-log availability. Voluntary gaps remain explicit and sponsors still need independent dependency assurance.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that evaluating only the final text output of an agentic device misses risks arising along the action path, including planning, tool selection, permission boundaries, memory/retrieval provenance, multi-agent propagation, tool-output validation, prompt injection via retrieved or tool content, and the handling of irreversible actions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sequence-level evaluation of agentic behavior across the full action path, including tool-output validation, prompt-injection resistance, confirmation of irreversible actions, rollback, and post-action state checks, with acceptance criteria applied to the entire action path rather than the final output alone.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment focuses on permission boundaries, tool selection, and confirmation of irreversible actions, i.e., the scope of authority an agent exercises without human review.
gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: It treats prompt injection through retrieved or tool content and tool-output validation as safety-relevant evaluation criteria rather than separate security matters.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: It emphasizes irreversible actions, rollback, and post-action state checks, pointing to harms that materialize in the executed workflow rather than in the output text.

positions.public_summary: Welcomes FDA's focus on agentic devices, but argues evaluation must cover the full action sequence, not just final outputs: planning, tool selection, permission boundaries, retrieval provenance, multi-agent propagation, tool-output validation, prompt injection, irreversible-action confirmation, rollback, and post-action state checks, with acceptance criteria spanning the entire
positions.source_passage: BCR response. Evaluate sequence-level realization: planning, tool selection, permission boundaries, memory/retrieval provenance, multi-agent propagation, tool-output validation, prompt injection through retrieved/tool content, irreversible-action confirmation, rollback, and post-action state checks. Acceptance criteria apply to the entire action path, not only the final text output.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage, part of a numbered set of framework principles, treats changes to the model, tools, deployment environment, intended use, permissions, or safety behavior as triggers that should reopen the affected portions of the risk/qualification analysis, and holds that risk controls should not be considered effective until post-control evidence demonstrates closure.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that any change to model, tooling, environment, intended use, permissions, or safety behavior reopen the affected assessment branches with a documented change-delta and requalification record, and that assigned controls only be credited once post-control evidence demonstrates closure.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The passage treats changes in intended use, permissions, and safety behavior as change triggers requiring requalification, implying the device's behavioral envelope is not fixed at authorization.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It lists changes in the deployment environment and tooling as events that reopen assessment, extending change control beyond the manufacturer's model to site-level conditions.

positions.public_summary: This excerpt from a numbered framework proposes that any change to model, tools, environment, intended use, permissions, or safety behavior reopen affected assessment branches with a documented change-delta and requalification record, and that risk controls be credited only after post-control closure evidence.
positions.source_passage:
7 - Re-open on change If model, tool, environment, intended use, permissions, or safety behavior changes, reopen affected branches.
Change-delta + requalification record.
8 - Close only with evidence Do not credit assigned controls until post-control evidence demonstrates closure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter affirms that FDA has correctly identified benchmark contamination, saturation, and limited real-world representativeness as threats to the validity of benchmark-based evidence.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific change is requested; the commenter endorses FDA's pairing of non-clinical benchmarking with clinical confirmation and its offering of multiple evidence approaches of varying rigor.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's framing, agreeing that benchmark contamination, saturation, and limited real-world representativeness threaten validity, and that pairing non-clinical benchmarking with clinical confirmation across multiple evidence approaches is appropriate. No changes are requested.
positions.source_passage:
Correctly identifies benchmark contamination, saturation, and real-world representativeness as threats to validity.
 Correctly pairs non-clinical benchmarking with clinical confirmation and offers multiple evidence approaches.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter contends that the two-axis framework (device activity and consequence of an incorrect output) cannot by itself serve as a complete basis for regulatory determinations, noting that the discussion paper itself acknowledges further relevant dimensions.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage implies FDA should not treat the two-axis framework as a self-contained determinant of risk and should incorporate the additional dimensions the paper identifies, though no specific dimensions or mechanisms are named in the passage.
positions.public_summary: The commenter states the two-axis risk framework is not sufficient on its own as a complete regulatory determination tool, pointing out that FDA's own discussion paper identifies additional relevant risk dimensions. No specific alternative dimensions or framework changes are named.
positions.source_passage: The two-axis risk picture is not sufficient as a complete regulatory closure function because the paper itself identifies multiple additional dimensions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that the risk framework does not specify any systematic rule for how material dimensions interact, citing autonomy by consequence, tool use by granted permissions, user capability by output directiveness, and modification by monitoring intensity.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify explicit coupling rules governing how these interacting dimensions combine within the risk framework, rather than treating them as independent axes.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment identifies the interaction between user capability and output directiveness as an unaddressed coupling, implying risk depends on the user-device combination rather than the output alone.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment flags autonomy-by-consequence and tools-by-permissions interactions as lacking any specified rule, pointing to the scope of authority granted to an agentic system.

positions.public_summary: Comment asserts FDA's risk framework specifies no systematic rule for how interacting dimensions combine, including autonomy with consequence, tool use with permissions, user capability with directiveness, and modification with monitoring, and seeks explicit coupling rules for these interactions.
positions.source_passage: No systematic coupling rule is specified for autonomy x consequence, tools x permissions, user capability x directiveness, change x monitoring, and other material interactions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage flags as unresolved the absence of defined 'non-averagable' hard-gate conditions, i.e., catastrophic, irreversible, or unauthorized output branches that should not be offset by good average performance in aggregate metrics.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define explicit criteria for hard-gate closure so that catastrophic, irreversible, or unauthorized behavior branches are evaluated against pass/fail thresholds rather than averaged performance.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The passage isolates catastrophic and irreversible outcome branches as harms that aggregate performance averaging can conceal, implying they need separate pass/fail treatment.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It names 'unauthorized' branches as a distinct category requiring explicit criteria, pointing to device actions taken beyond sanctioned authority.

positions.public_summary: A terse checklist entry noting that FDA has not defined 'non-averagable' hard-gate conditions. The commenter treats explicit pass/fail criteria for catastrophic, irreversible, or unauthorized output branches—not averaged performance metrics—as an unresolved requirement. Position is stated only as an open item.
positions.source_passage:
Non-averagable hard-gate conditions are not yet defined.
...
Hard-gate closure Non-averagable catastrophic/irreversible/unauthorized branches have explicit criteria and pass.
OPEN

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter notes that the concept of meaningful human oversight remains undefined in operational terms, having not been translated into measurable criteria such as visibility into the system's actions, the scope of human authority, time available to intervene, override capability, and reversibility of actions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify meaningful human oversight as measurable criteria—visibility, authority, intervention time, override, and reversibility—so that oversight expectations for agentic GenAI-enabled devices can be assessed rather than asserted.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The passage centers on the unspecified scope of human authority, override capability, and reversibility when action is delegated to an autonomous system.
gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: It frames oversight as a property of the human-device arrangement (visibility, intervention time) rather than of the device output alone, which FDA's question does not operationalize.

positions.public_summary: Comment states that "meaningful human oversight" for agentic GenAI devices has not been reduced to measurable criteria, and identifies visibility, human authority, intervention time, override, and reversibility as dimensions FDA would need to specify for oversight expectations to be assessable.
positions.source_passage: Meaningful human oversight is not yet reduced to measurable visibility, authority, intervention time, override, and reversibility criteria.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter notes that while the discussion paper acknowledges benchmark construct validity as a problem, it does not establish a required, closed evidentiary chain linking benchmark performance to clinical confirmation and then to observed postmarket behavior.
positions.requested_fda_action: Close the proof chain by making the linkage from benchmark results to clinical confirmation and postmarket performance explicit and mandatory rather than acknowledged but unaddressed.
positions.public_summary: Commenter observes that FDA acknowledges benchmark construct validity concerns but does not require a closed evidentiary chain from benchmarking to clinical confirmation to postmarket behavior, and implies this linkage should be made explicit and mandatory.
positions.source_passage: Benchmark construct validity is recognized as a problem but a mandatory proof chain from benchmark -> clinical confirmation -> postmarket behavior is not closed.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter notes that the process for selecting a clinical confirmation approach is left open-ended and that there is no deterministic rule for escalating to a more rigorous confirmation method when residual uncertainty is not resolved.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage implies FDA should specify a determinate escalation rule governing how clinical confirmation approaches are selected and when unresolved residual uncertainty requires a higher-rigor confirmation method.
positions.public_summary: The commenter observes that FDA's approach leaves clinical confirmation selection open-ended and provides no deterministic rule for escalating to more rigorous confirmation when residual uncertainty remains, implying a need for clearer escalation criteria. The passage is brief and largely diagnostic.
positions.source_passage: Clinical confirmation selection remains open and lacks a deterministic escalation rule for unresolved residuals.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage asserts that there is no closed rule governing independence and transportability when synthetic and real-world evidence are combined, implying that conditions for pooling such evidence into a single performance estimate are undefined.
positions.requested_fda_action: Not stated explicitly; the passage implies FDA would need to define criteria addressing independence and transportability before synthetic and real-world evidence are combined.
positions.public_summary: A brief remark stating that combining synthetic and real-world evidence lacks a settled rule for independence and transportability. The passage identifies this analytic gap in FDA's framing but does not state a clear position or a specific requested action.
positions.source_passage: Synthetic/real evidence combination lacks a closed independence/transportability rule.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage observes that requirements for detecting third-party foundation model identity/version changes and for holding or rolling back to a prior model state are not currently mandatory, implying a gap in assurance when model changes originate outside the device manufacturer.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage does not state a specific request; it notes only the absence of mandatory third-party model identity/change-detection and hold/rollback requirements, which could imply an interest in making such controls required.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The passage centers on the lack of mandatory controls for detecting and responding to changes in an externally supplied foundation model, a supplier-quality assurance issue.

positions.public_summary: Brief observation that requirements for third-party foundation model identity and change detection, and for hold or rollback capability, are not currently mandatory. The passage identifies this as a gap but states no explicit position or recommended FDA action.
positions.source_passage: Third-party model identity/change detection and hold/rollback requirements are not yet mandatory.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter observes that PCCP concepts, as currently framed, are not articulated as a measurable envelope of permissible boundaries and deltas, leaving change limits imprecise for GenAI-enabled devices whose future modifications cannot be fully prespecified.
positions.requested_fda_action: Express PCCP or equivalent change-control concepts as a quantifiable boundary-and-delta envelope, so that allowable modification limits and deviations can be measured and monitored.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment calls for change control to be defined as a measurable boundary-delta envelope, which goes beyond prespecified modification lists toward bounding a device's permissible behavioral range.

positions.public_summary: Brief comment noting that FDA's PCCP concepts are not currently articulated as a measurable boundary-and-delta envelope. Implies change-control approaches for generative AI should define quantifiable limits on permissible modification rather than qualitative descriptions. Little supporting detail is provided.
positions.source_passage: PCCP concepts are not yet expressed as a measurable boundary-delta envelope.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that evaluation of agentic GenAI devices requires specific, explicit elements not spelled out in the discussion paper, namely definition of action states, tool permissions, identification of irreversible action nodes, and verification after actions are taken.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add explicit requirements to agentic device evaluation covering action-state definition, tool-permission scoping, irreversible-node identification, and post-action verification.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The call for explicit action-state and tool-permission requirements concerns the scope of authority delegated to an autonomous agent to act and use tools.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: Identifying irreversible action nodes and verifying actions after execution addresses harm arising from actions taken in operation rather than from output accuracy alone.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts FDA's attention to agentic devices but asks that evaluation include explicit requirements: defined action states, scoped tool permissions, identification of irreversible action points, and post-action verification—elements not specified in the discussion paper's agentic oversight discussion.
positions.source_passage: Agentic evaluation needs explicit action-state, tool-permission, irreversible-node, and post-action verification requirements.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that postmarket monitoring as described lacks defined accountability for residual risk, explicit thresholds for triggering action, logic accounting for time-to-harm, and mechanisms for automatically reopening or requalifying a device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require postmarket monitoring programs to designate residual risk owners, specify quantitative trigger thresholds, incorporate harm-timing logic, and provide for automatic reassessment or requalification when triggers are met.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The call for named 'residual owners' addresses who remains accountable for unresolved risk once monitoring roles are shared across parties.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: The reference to 'harm-time logic' introduces the timing of harm accrual as a factor monitoring triggers must account for, which FDA's cadence-focused framing does not fully capture.

positions.public_summary: Accepts postmarket monitoring in principle but argues FDA's approach is incomplete, calling for designated owners of residual risk, defined trigger thresholds, logic reflecting time-to-harm, and automatic reopening or requalification when triggers are met.
positions.source_passage: Postmarket monitoring needs residual owners, trigger thresholds, harm-time logic, and automatic re-open/requalification.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter regards the discussion paper as a sound starting point but treats its concepts as incomplete, describing the policy concept as 'PARTIAL' until the proposed controls are actually implemented and empirically demonstrated.
positions.requested_fda_action: Convert the paper's open questions into a traceable 'realization-and-closure' architecture, and treat the framework as provisional until the associated controls are implemented and supported by empirical demonstration.
positions.public_summary: Concluding statement calls FDA's discussion paper a strong starting point rather than rejecting it, but proposes restructuring its open questions into a traceable realization-and-closure architecture and treats the policy concept as incomplete until the proposed controls are implemented and empirically demonstrated.
positions.source_passage: Final BCR conclusion. FDA's discussion paper is a strong starting point. BCR does not reject it; BCR converts the open questions into a traceable realization-and-closure architecture. The policy concept remains PARTIAL until the proposed controls are implemented and empirically demonstrated.
